draft.title: Simultaneous equations
card: Substitution
Rearrange one equation to give y (or x), then put it into the other. Example: y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 11 give 3x + 2x + 1 = 11, so x = 2 and y = 5.
Elimination
Add or subtract the equations to remove one variable. Example: x + y = 7 and x − y = 3 add to give 2x = 10, so x = 5 and y = 2.
A line can meet a parabola. Substitute the line into the parabola to get a quadratic, then solve it. There can be two solutions, one or none.
Find y for each x using the line's rule. The answer is a point (x, y), so always give both coordinates.
draft.remember: Combine the equations to get one variable, solve it, then go back for the other.

a.q: Solve y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 11 together. What is the solution (x, y)?
a.why: Substituting gives 3x + 2x + 1 = 11, so 5x = 10 and x = 2. Then y = 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. (5, 2) has the coordinates swapped.
a.clue: Replace y in the second equation with 2x + 1.

b.q: The line y = x + 2 meets the parabola y = x². Where do they meet?
b.why: Set x² = x + 2, so x² − x − 2 = 0, which factorises as (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0. So x = 2 or x = −1, and the points are (2, 4) and (−1, 1). (2, 4) only is tempting, but the quadratic has two solutions.
b.clue: Put x + 2 equal to x², then factorise.

card: Substitution

a.q: Solve \(y = 3x - 2\) and \(2x + y = 13\) together. What is the solution \((x, y)\)?
a.why: Substituting gives \(2x + 3x - 2 = 13\), so \(5x = 15\) and \(x = 3\). Then \(y = 3 \times 3 - 2 = 7\), which also checks in \(2 \times 3 + 7 = 13\). \((7, 3)\) has the coordinates swapped.

b.q: The line \(y = x + 2\) meets the parabola \(y = x^{2}\). Where do they meet?
